title: The Knee and the Nucleus: from a Volhynian shtetl to the floor of the world
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Slavuta, birth in the Volhynian shtetl
stops.date_confidence: attested in Reese's authorized biography and in Guild materials. A minority of encyclopedic entries give 1900 or 1902; the contradiction is left standing.
stops.campa: In Slavuta, on the Horyn in the Volhynia Governorate of the Russian Empire, a first son is born to Sheindel and Mordechai Feldenkrais. The father binds books and trades grain and keeps company with the Hovevei Zion men who talk about Palestine as a place a person might actually go to. They name the boy Moshe. The town is a printing town, Hasidic, and poor, and nothing in it suggests that this child will end his life explaining to Californians on a gymnasium floor how a human being learns to stand up.
suggested_refs: Jewish community records of Slavuta, Volhynia Governorate, for 1904
sources: Mark Reese, Marvelous Beyond Counting: Moshe Feldenkrais, A Life (2015)

stops.name: Baranovichi, the family moves north
stops.date_confidence: no source dates the relocation. Wikipedia attaches no year to it; an earlier research pass interpolated 1912 and it is kept here only as an ordering device inside Reese's loose c.1912-1918 range. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The family settles in Baranovichi, a railway junction of the western empire. Moshe goes to cheder and then to a Russian gymnasium, two years of it, and studies Hebrew and the Zionist argument alongside the official curriculum. He works geometry out of library books on his own, and the habit shows itself early and never afterwards leaves him: he would rather derive a thing than be told it. War comes through the town in 1914 and keeps coming through it, and the schooling stops there.
suggested_refs: Baranovichi gymnasium enrolment records, not located

stops.name: Baranovichi, bar mitzvah in a war zone
stops.date_confidence: the bar mitzvah is attested; no source gives its date. 1917 is arithmetic from a 1904 birth and is not testimony. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He is called to the Torah in a town that has changed hands and armies. The empire that governs Baranovichi is dissolving, the front has crossed Belorussia twice, and the Jewish towns to the south are beginning to burn. He is thirteen, with two years of gymnasium, a workable Hebrew, and a boy's map of a country he has never seen. Men back from the front say the roads south are open, in the sense that nobody is watching them. In the youth movement they talk about walking there. He is one of the ones who means it.
suggested_refs: Records of the Zionist youth movement in Baranovichi during the First World War

stops.name: Baranovichi, the road south at fourteen
stops.date_confidence: 1918 is attested for the emigration; the month is a placement. [R] for the walk itself, which rests on Feldenkrais's own later retelling as relayed by Reese. Two research lenses tagged this identical event differently, one attested and one reconstructed; harmonized down to reconstructed.
stops.campa: At fourteen he leaves. The telling that survives is his own, given decades later to students in California and to interviewers who wanted a founder's story: that he set out from Baranovichi at the head of a small band of Zionist youngsters, that he carried a pistol and a book of mathematics, and that he was the one who knew the way. Nothing independent confirms any of it. What is certain is that a boy of fourteen left this town in 1918 and reached Palestine, and that no adult brought him.
suggested_refs: Feldenkrais's autobiographical remarks in Awareness Through Movement lectures and later interviews

stops.name: Odessa, the Black Sea and the emigrant road
stops.date_confidence: [R] entirely. Odessa is reconstructed from the standard emigration routes of the period; the actual stages of his own route are undocumented, and this stop is an inference wearing a coordinate.
stops.campa: South through Ukraine in the year Ukraine has no settled government, toward the port that has been sending Jews out of the empire for forty years. Odessa in 1918 changes hands like a coin, German troops in it and Bolsheviks under it, and the harbour still working. Emigrants pool money for passage and sleep in the sheds along the water. Whether he passes through here is a reconstruction and not a record: this is the road everyone took, and the road he took is written down nowhere.
suggested_refs: Odessa emigration and passage records for 1918-1919, not located
sources: General accounts of Second and Third Aliyah emigration routes

stops.name: Jaffa, coming ashore with nothing
stops.date_confidence: sources disagree: some give late 1918, others 1919. The contradiction is left standing. 1919 is chosen only so the arrival sits after the journey, and adjudicates nothing. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: After something like a year on the road he lands at Jaffa, port of a country that has just stopped being Ottoman and has not yet decided what it is. There is no money and no family waiting on the stones. He is fifteen, or sixteen, depending on which arrival year one believes, and he speaks a Hebrew learned out of a schoolbook in Belorussia and is about to discover how much of it works on a wharf. The Third Aliyah is coming ashore around him and looks much the same.
suggested_refs: Mandate and Ottoman port registers at Jaffa, 1918-1919

segments.name: The Yishuv: Survey, Jiu-Jitsu, the Knee

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the labourer years
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The laborer years are attested in outline only; the year is a placement inside the 1919-1928 range Reese gives. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He goes to work with his hands, because that is the work there is: construction, and then surveying, which pays better and requires arithmetic, and which he teaches himself. The halutzim around him are raising a city on the sand dunes north of Jaffa and calling it Tel Aviv. At night he borrows books and works through mathematics and physics alone, the Baranovichi habit intact, and there is not one teacher in the country who knows he is doing it, nor any examination he is working toward.
suggested_refs: Labour records of the Tel Aviv building trades in the early 1920s

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the Gymnasia Herzliya diploma
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1925 in Wikipedia; month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: The high school diploma comes at twenty-one, taken at the Gymnasia Herzliya, and he has prepared for it himself while working. It is the first piece of paper of his life. Every certificate that follows, an engineering diploma from Paris and a doctorate in physics from the Sorbonne, sits on top of a secondary education assembled out of borrowed books at the ends of working days. He will spend his teaching life insisting that a person can learn what nobody has taught them.
suggested_refs: Gymnasia Herzliya examination records for 1925

stops.name: Palestine, cartographer to the British survey
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1925; the month is a placement chosen to separate this from the diploma. The pin is Tel Aviv generally, since no survey office address is established.
stops.campa: The survey office of the Mandate takes him on as a cartographer, and the boy who worked geometry out of library books is paid to put a country onto paper. In the same year he begins studying self-defense and jiu-jitsu out of manuals, since there is no instructor within reach. In the Palestine of the middle twenties the technical trades of an empire are open to whoever can pass the examination, and a young man learns to fight because not knowing how has a price attached to it.
suggested_refs: Survey of Palestine personnel records for the 1920s

stops.name: Tel Aviv, teaching the Haganah to fall
stops.date_confidence: [R], from Reese and from Feldenkrais's own early self-defense pamphlets. The dating is loose, c.1929-1930; month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The riots of 1929 make the question practical, and he teaches what he taught himself: jiu-jitsu out of books, adapted for men who have to hold a street. He writes it down and publishes it, a self-defense manual in Hebrew by a surveyor of twenty-five who has never trained under anybody. Six years later he will be on a Paris mat under a Japanese master, finding out how much of it was wrong and how much he had guessed correctly from the diagrams. For now he is teaching men to fall who have never been taught by anyone at all.
suggested_refs: Feldenkrais's early Hebrew self-defense pamphlets, not located

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the knee on the football field
stops.date_confidence: [R]. Wikipedia gives 1929 for the soccer injury; the month is a placement. The injury's later role in the work is narrated by Feldenkrais himself and is not independently documented.
stops.campa: A football match, a bad landing, and the left knee goes. It heals as knees healed then, which is to say imperfectly and with a promise to come back. He is twenty-five, and he does not go to a doctor about it. The decades of studying his own movement start from this afternoon, and so does the surgeon he will refuse in Paris eight years from now. The thousands who will one day lie on floors following his instructions are never told that the curriculum began on a football pitch in Tel Aviv.
suggested_refs: Feldenkrais's own accounts of the knee in Awareness Through Movement and later interviews

segments.name: Paris: the Radium Institute and the Mat

stops.name: Marseille, landing in France
stops.date_confidence: 1930 is attested for the emigration to France. [R] for Marseille itself, which is inferred from period convention and from Reese rather than confirmed for this voyage. Month is a placement.
stops.campa: He sails from Palestine to France to get the education the country he helped build cannot give him. Marseille is where Mediterranean crossings ended in those years and it is where the accounts put him, though nothing confirms the ship or the quay. He is twenty-five, carrying a self-made high school diploma, a surveyor's hands, a damaged knee, and a Hebrew pamphlet on hand-to-hand fighting. Paris is a night on a train to the north, and he takes it.
suggested_refs: Passenger manifests for Haifa or Jaffa to Marseille crossings, 1930

stops.name: Paris, the École Spéciale des Travaux Publics
stops.date_confidence: the school and the diploma are attested; enrolment in 1930 is inferred from the arrival and the 1933 diploma. Coordinate corrected: the school stood on rue Thénard in the Latin Quarter from 1898 through the 1930s, not at the modern Cachan campus.
stops.campa: He enrols in the engineering school on rue Thénard, in the quarter where the Latin schools have stood for seven centuries, and takes odd jobs to pay for it. The curriculum is public works: strength of materials, structures, the mechanics of things that must not fall over. He is learning at a desk, formally, the physics of a body under load. It will be twenty years before he applies any of it to a body that is not a bridge, and he has no idea yet that this is what he is being trained for.
suggested_refs: École Spéciale des Travaux Publics enrolment registers, 1930-1933

stops.name: Paris, the engineering diploma
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1933; month and day unknown and defaulted. Note that the doctorate in physics is frequently printed with this same year, which the record does not support.
stops.campa: Three years and the diploma is his. In the same year he crosses into the other Paris that will hold him, the laboratory city of the Curies and the mat rooms of the first French judo, and the two run in parallel from here to the war. He is an engineer with a certificate, which in 1933 means work is available. He does not take work. He goes further in instead: a doctorate begun, and a place in a laboratory where the periodic table is currently being rewritten.
suggested_refs: Diploma records of the École Spéciale des Travaux Publics for 1933

stops.name: Institut du Radium, assistant to Joliot-Curie
stops.date_confidence: 1933 is attested for the start of the Institut du Radium work; the month is a placement. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from the existing corpus pin for the Institut du Radium, which sits about 100 m from Wikipedia's value for the building.
stops.campa: On rue Pierre et Marie Curie he becomes a research assistant to Frédéric Joliot-Curie and works in the laboratory through the years of artificial radioactivity and the first approaches to fission. The building is the centre of French nuclear physics and it is run by a couple who will share a Nobel Prize within eighteen months. He is a Jewish surveyor from Tel Aviv with a public-works diploma, and he is at the bench. Tradition adds Marie Curie among his teachers. She holds her chair until she dies in July 1934, so it is possible, and no roster puts him in her lecture room.
suggested_refs: Institut Curie staff records for the Joliot-Curie laboratory, 1933-1939

stops.name: Paris, Jigoro Kano comes to the city
stops.date_confidence: attested for September 1933. The coordinate is a declared central-Paris placeholder: no dojo or meeting address is established in any reachable source.
stops.campa: The founder of judo passes through Paris and Feldenkrais meets him. Kano is seventy-three and travelling Europe to plant his art in it. The young physicist shows him the jiu-jitsu he assembled from manuals in Tel Aviv, and Kano, by every account of the meeting, is interested rather than dismissive. From here the self-taught fighting stops and the trained fighting starts, under Kano's men in France. He is twenty-nine and beginning again at the bottom of a discipline he had thought he already knew.
suggested_refs: Kodokan records of Kano Jigoro's European tour, September 1933

stops.name: Paris, Kawaishi on the mat
stops.date_confidence: corrected. The standard telling starts this training in 1933, but Kawaishi taught in Liverpool from c.1928 and London from 1931 and reached Paris only in 1935. Who taught Feldenkrais between 1933 and 1935 is an open gap. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Mikinosuke Kawaishi arrives in Paris to teach, having spent seven years putting judo into English cities first, and Feldenkrais trains under him. Kawaishi teaches Europeans by numbering the throws, a concession to students with no Japanese and no patience, and the concession works: France takes to judo faster than anywhere else on the continent. On the mat Feldenkrais watches grown men acquire a skill by being handed the order of its parts. He is taking notes he will use forty years later.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Mikinosuke Kawaishi', on the 1935 move to Paris

stops.name: Paris, the black belt and the Jiu-Jitsu Club de France
stops.date_confidence: 1936 is given by Wikipedia, which flags its own judo dates as uncited. The club's continued existence is [R]. Coordinate is a declared central-Paris placeholder. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He takes shodan, among the first Europeans to hold a judo black belt, and with Kawaishi founds the Jiu-Jitsu Club de France, which outlives them both. He writes on the subject as he writes on every subject, systematically and with diagrams. In these same years he runs experiments in a nuclear laboratory by day and throws men onto canvas at night, and nobody in either building treats the combination as remarkable, because he never presents it as one.
suggested_refs: Fédération Française de Judo historical records on the founding of the Jiu-Jitsu Club de France

stops.name: Paris, the knee refuses the surgeon
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The chronology comes from Feldenkrais's own retrospective narration; one research lens tagged it attested while conceding in the same note that it was undocumented, and it is corrected down here. The date is a placement inside c.1936-1939.
stops.campa: Judo finishes what football began. The knee gives out, and the surgeons offer an operation with, they tell him, about even odds of leaving him worse. He declines it. He is an engineer, a physicist and a black belt, which gives him three separate vocabularies for a joint under load, and he turns all three on his own leg. He begins studying how he actually moves: on the floor, slowly, watching what he does in the instant before the pain arrives. Nobody has asked him to do this and nobody is watching him do it.
stops.quote: No matter how closely we look, it is difficult to find a mental act that can take place without the support of some physical function.
stops.quote_source: Widely attributed to Feldenkrais and commonly assigned to The Elusive Obvious (1981); edition unconfirmed, not verified against a primary text.
suggested_refs: Feldenkrais's account of the knee and the refused surgery in Awareness Through Movement
sources: Feldenkrais's own later accounts in interviews

stops.name: Institut du Radium, judo for the Joliot-Curies
stops.date_confidence: 1938 is attested for the second dan and for the pupils named. Wikipedia flags the judo dates as uncited within its own article. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Second-degree black belt, and his pupils now include Frédéric and Irène Joliot-Curie, whose laboratory he works in, along with the physicist Bertrand Goldschmidt, who will later help build a bomb. In the same rooms where induced radioactivity was found in 1934, two of its finders are learning breakfalls from their own research assistant. He teaches them to go down without damage, which is the only subject he will ever really teach, and which nobody including him has noticed yet.
suggested_refs: Bertrand Goldschmidt's memoirs on the Radium Institute years

stops.name: Clermont-Ferrand, the laboratory scatters
stops.date_confidence: [R] for Feldenkrais's presence in the dispersal specifically. The move of the French nuclear work toward Clermont-Ferrand is documented; his part in it is not. Month is a placement at the declaration of war.
stops.campa: War is declared and the laboratory disperses, its people and its dangerous stock moving south toward Clermont-Ferrand ahead of the German advance. What Feldenkrais does in these months is not documented anywhere reachable. He is a Polish-born Jew inside a French nuclear programme, which by the following June will be two separate reasons to be somewhere other than Paris. The accounts that put him in the convoy are repeating a story, and the story has a hole here that nobody fills.
suggested_refs: Histories of the French nuclear laboratory's 1939-1940 evacuation
sources: Accounts of the Joliot-Curie, von Halban and Kowarski evacuation

stops.name: Bordeaux, the exodus and the heavy water
stops.date_confidence: [R], and this is the largest correction in the file. Wikipedia has Feldenkrais fleeing with heavy-water research material for the British Admiralty and War Office. The documented carriers were Hans von Halban and Lew Kowarski, aboard the SS Broompark out of Bordeaux on 19 June 1940. He appears in none of the operational accounts. The contradiction is flagged, not resolved.
stops.campa: France falls, and everyone who cannot stay goes to the Atlantic ports. The Broompark sails from Bordeaux on the nineteenth of June carrying Halban, Kowarski, the world's stock of heavy water, a gram of radium, and thirty-three unnamed scientists and technicians. The story told ever after is that Feldenkrais carried the heavy water to England himself. The histories of that cargo do not contain his name. He may have been one of the thirty-three, and that is the whole of what can honestly be said.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'SS Broompark' and 'Hans von Halban', on the June 1940 heavy-water evacuation

stops.name: Falmouth, coming ashore in England
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The Broompark landed at Falmouth on 21 June 1940; whether Feldenkrais was aboard is unresolved, so this stop dates his English landfall by that ship's arrival and declares the assumption rather than hiding it.
stops.campa: Cornwall, in the week the war becomes British and nothing else. He arrives with what a refugee arrives with, which in his case is his training. There is no country to go back to: Poland is occupied, France is occupied, and Palestine sits at the far end of a sea full of submarines. Within months the Admiralty will find a use for a physicist who understands sound in water, and he will spend the war working against the boats that closed the sea behind him.
suggested_refs: Falmouth port arrival records for June 1940
sources: General accounts of the 1940 refugee crossings to England

stops.name: London, taken on by the Admiralty
stops.date_confidence: Admiralty service from 1940 to 1946 is attested; the month is a placement. Coordinate corrected to the Admiralty building itself, since an earlier research pass pinned Downing Street and Whitehall.
stops.campa: He is taken on as a science officer of the British Admiralty, which is a remarkable posting for a stateless Jew off a refugee crossing, and it happens because the war needs exactly what he can do. His subject is submarines: how to find them, and what to do to them once found. The engineering degree, the physics doctorate and the surveyor's arithmetic are all in use at once. He serves six years and holds patents afterwards for improvements that came out of the work.
suggested_refs: Admiralty scientific service personnel files, 1940-1946; Feldenkrais's sonar patents, numbers not located

stops.name: Fairlie, sonar on the Firth of Clyde
stops.date_confidence: attested: anti-submarine weaponry at Fairlie, Scotland. Corrected in two directions, since one research lens moved this work to London and another downgraded Fairlie to tradition. Coordinate corrected by about 0.5 km. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The Admiralty's anti-submarine establishment sits on the Ayrshire coast, looking out at the Firth of Clyde where the convoys form. Here he works on detection and on the weapons that follow detection. The problem is sound in cold water and the geometry of a thing nobody can see. He is very far north, in a country at war, doing mathematics for a navy. He is thirty-seven years old and has not yet given a single lesson of the work he will be remembered for.
suggested_refs: Admiralty anti-submarine establishment records at Fairlie, Ayrshire

stops.name: London, Practical Unarmed Combat
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The 1942 publication is attested by the book itself; the London pin is a publishing address rather than a documented place of writing. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: For the Home Guard, men with pitchforks and a real expectation of German paratroopers, he writes a manual of hand-to-hand fighting. It is the third time in his life he has written down how to defend yourself and the first time in a language that is neither Hebrew nor French. The Tel Aviv pamphlet was guesswork from diagrams. This one is Kawaishi's judo stripped to what a frightened civilian with one evening a week can actually be taught to do. The invasion it is written against never comes, and the book stays in print regardless.
suggested_refs: Moshe Feldenkrais, Practical Unarmed Combat (1942)

stops.name: Fairlie, the deck and the old knee
stops.date_confidence: [R]. Wikipedia dates the wartime re-aggravation loosely; 1943 is a placement inside the Admiralty years. The narration is Feldenkrais's own and is not independently documented. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The knee goes again, on wet steel decks that will not hold still. There is no Paris surgeon to refuse this time and no time to be laid up, so the private experiment of 1937 becomes a daily discipline: lying down, moving slowly, finding the pattern of effort that runs ahead of the pain and taking it apart piece by piece. He reads physiology, neurology, anatomy, the literature of hypnosis and of yoga. The subject of the study is one left leg and the researcher is its owner.
stops.quote: Learning to inhibit unwanted contractions of muscles that function without, or in spite of, our will, is the main task in coordinated action.
stops.quote_source: Widely attributed to Feldenkrais, phrasing consistent with Body and Mature Behavior (1949); edition unconfirmed, not verified against a primary text.
suggested_refs: Feldenkrais's wartime notebooks, not located

stops.name: London, the first classes
stops.date_confidence: attested that he leaves Admiralty service in 1946 and begins lecturing and running experimental classes; the classes themselves are [R]. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The war ends, the Admiralty releases him, and he takes work in private industry while doing what he actually wants to do, which is talk about what he found in his own leg. He lectures. He runs experimental classes for whoever turns up. He sits on the International Judo Committee and studies the art the way a scientist studies it, asking not how the throw is done but how a nervous system comes to be able to do it. Nobody yet calls any of this a method.
suggested_refs: Records of Feldenkrais's London lectures and experimental classes, 1946-1950

stops.name: London, the reading of the somatic teachers
stops.date_confidence: attested that he studies these figures during the London years. 1948 is a placement, since no source dates the reading. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He works through the people who got there before him: Gurdjieff and his movements, F. Matthias Alexander on the use of the self, William Bates on the eyes, and Elsa Gindler, whose Berlin room taught a generation of Europeans to notice what they were doing while they were doing it. He is not a disciple of any of them. He is a physicist reading the literature, and this is the literature, and there is no journal that prints it and no chair anywhere that teaches it.
stops.quote: Our breathing reflects every emotional or physical effort and every disturbance.
stops.quote_source: Widely attributed to Feldenkrais, consistent with themes in Body and Mature Behavior (1949); edition unconfirmed, not verified against a primary text.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Somatics', on the parallel somatic pioneers of the early twentieth century

stops.name: London, Body and Mature Behavior
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1949; month and day unknown and defaulted. Later editions and translations were not verified this pass.
stops.campa: The book comes out with a subtitle that reads like an inventory of everything on his mind at once: a study of anxiety, sex, gravitation and learning. The argument is that posture is not a fact about a skeleton but a habit of a nervous system, that the habit was learned, and that whatever was learned can be learned differently. He is forty-five. He has published on radiation and on unarmed combat. Nothing in the new book is offered as therapy. This is the one that starts the rest of it.
stops.quote: In order to change our mode of action, we must change the image of ourselves that we carry within us.
stops.quote_source: Widely attributed to Feldenkrais and commonly assigned to Body and Mature Behavior (1949); edition unconfirmed, not verified against a primary text.
suggested_refs: Moshe Feldenkrais, Body and Mature Behavior: A Study of Anxiety, Sex, Gravitation and Learning (London, 1949)

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the return to Israel
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1951; month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: He comes back to a country that did not exist when he left it. He was here when it was dunes and a survey office and a Mandate. It is three years old now, at war with its neighbours, and short of every kind of person it needs. He is forty-seven, a doctor of physics with an Admiralty war behind him, and the new state has an obvious use for him. The work on the leg comes back in his luggage, unfinished, unnamed, and by now more than twenty years old.
suggested_refs: Israeli immigration records for 1951

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the army's electronics department
stops.date_confidence: attested that he directs the Israel Defense Forces Electronics Department before teaching full-time; 1954 is the year given for the transition. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He directs the electronics department of the Israeli army's research establishment and does for the new state's defence what he did for the Royal Navy. It is the last post he will hold in physics. At the end of it he walks away from the discipline that carried him from a Tel Aviv survey office to the Institut du Radium, and sets up as a teacher of movement at fifty. No institution stands behind him. There is no credential for the thing he intends to do, because there is not yet a discipline with the authority to issue one.
suggested_refs: Israel Defense Forces science corps records for the early 1950s

stops.name: Zurich, to Heinrich Jacoby
stops.date_confidence: no source gives a year for the Swiss study. The existing corpus places it at 1954, inside Jacoby's settled Zurich period after his 1947 residency; the research pool for this file placed it in 1948 alongside the London reading. Both are placements, neither is sourced, and the conflict is left standing. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from the corpus.
stops.campa: He travels to Switzerland to work with Heinrich Jacoby, who taught for fifteen years alongside Elsa Gindler in Berlin and has not been able to enter Germany since 1933. What Jacoby has to hand over is a Berlin room kept alive in a Swiss classroom by one of the two people who made it. Feldenkrais takes the tuition directly, at the source, having already worked through the rest of the somatic literature alone. No year is written down for this. It happened, and where it sits in the life is a guess.
suggested_refs: Heinrich Jacoby's Zurich teaching records; the Gindler-Jacoby archive
sources: elsa_gindler.journey.json, stop 'Zurich, Feldenkrais comes to Jacoby'

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the practice on the floor
stops.date_confidence: attested in outline that he opens a Tel Aviv practice in the 1950s and develops the two forms there; the specific year is a placement. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He opens a practice, and the two halves of the work take their names. Functional Integration is done with the hands, one person at a time on a low table, the teacher moving them in ways their nervous system has forgotten were available. Awareness Through Movement is done by a whole room on the floor, following instructions spoken aloud, very slowly, with the eyes shut. Neither one is exercise and neither one is therapy. Both are lessons, and he insists on the word.
stops.quote: Movement is life. Life is a process. Improve the quality of the process and you improve the quality of life itself.
stops.quote_source: Widely attributed to Feldenkrais in quotation compilations, likely from Awareness Through Movement (1972) or The Elusive Obvious (1981); no edition or page located, not verified against a primary text.
suggested_refs: Feldenkrais's Tel Aviv studio records; the Alexander Yanai lesson recordings
sources: Feldenkrais, Body and Mature Behavior (1949) and later works

stops.name: Tel Aviv, Mia Segal
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1957; month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: A young woman comes to him and stays thirty years. Mia Segal becomes the first person other than Feldenkrais who can do the work, which is the first evidence that it is a method and not a talent belonging to one pair of hands. She learns it the way he made it, by being moved rather than by being told. She will be beside him in California twenty years later, when the trainings run to hundreds of students at a time and he can no longer put his hands on all of them himself.
suggested_refs: Mia Segal's own accounts of thirty years assisting Feldenkrais

stops.name: Tel Aviv beach, Ben-Gurion upside down
stops.date_confidence: 1957 is attested for the Ben-Gurion training. [R] for the specific beach; the central Tel Aviv beachfront is an approximation. Corrected: an earlier research pass placed this at Sde Boker in the Negev, wrong for a serving Prime Minister based in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv.
stops.campa: The Prime Minister of Israel is seventy and cannot get out of a chair unaided, and he sends for the movement teacher. Feldenkrais gives him lessons. The photograph that comes out of it, David Ben-Gurion standing on his head on a Tel Aviv beach in swimming trunks, goes round the world and does more for the method in Israel than any book of his ever will. Ben-Gurion had said that he wanted to be able to stand on his head. That was the brief, and it was met.
suggested_refs: Israeli press photo archives for the Ben-Gurion headstand, 1957

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the first thirteen
stops.date_confidence: attested: the first teacher-training cohort, thirteen students, Tel Aviv, 1969 to 1971. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He trains teachers for the first time, thirteen of them, over three years in Tel Aviv. He is sixty-five, has been developing the work alone for thirty years, and until now it has existed only in his own hands and in Segal's. Thirteen people are now carrying it. The international profession that follows, with its guilds and its certifications and its literature, comes out of this room. He supervises the whole of it himself, one student at a time, in Hebrew.
suggested_refs: Records of the first Tel Aviv teacher training, 1969-1971

stops.name: Big Sur, Esalen and the American room
stops.date_confidence: attested: an Awareness Through Movement programme at the Esalen Institute in 1972. Month and day defaulted. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from the corpus, which had already corrected two research lenses that put Esalen several kilometres out in the Pacific.
stops.campa: On the cliff at Big Sur he presents Awareness Through Movement to the American human potential movement, which has been waiting for him without knowing his name. The room is full of people who have already met Gurdjieff's ideas and the Gindler line by way of Charlotte Selver, and who recognise the grammar at once. What Feldenkrais adds is the same territory walked by an engineer: no mysticism, a floor, an instruction spoken slowly, and a nervous system treated as a machine that learns.
stops.quote: I believe that the unity of mind and body is an objective reality. They are not just parts somehow related to each other, but an inseparable whole while functioning. A brain without a body could not think.
stops.quote_source: Widely attributed to Feldenkrais and commonly assigned to The Elusive Obvious (1981); edition unconfirmed, not verified against a primary text.
suggested_refs: Esalen Institute programme records for 1972

stops.name: San Francisco, Lone Mountain College
stops.date_confidence: attested: 65 teachers over four summers, 1975 to 1978, at Lone Mountain College. Month set to the summer session. Coordinate corrected from two different wrong pins offered by earlier lenses, one of them a bare San Francisco centroid.
stops.campa: Four summers on a hill in the western half of San Francisco, in the buildings of a Catholic women's college that will lose its name to the University of San Francisco before the training is over. Sixty-five teachers come out of it, the first professional cohort in North America. He is seventy-one when it starts. What began as one man's refusal of a knee operation on a Paris floor now has a curriculum and a continent, forty years later and half a world from where he started it.

stops.name: Amherst, the largest cohort
stops.date_confidence: attested: 235 students at Hampshire College from 1980. Corrected: one research lens named the University of Massachusetts Amherst, a different institution about seven kilometres north, contradicting its own chronology. Month set to the summer session.
stops.campa: Two hundred and thirty-five students enrol for the summer training at Hampshire College in Massachusetts, the largest group he has ever taught at once. Four summers are planned. He teaches two of them. The tapes made in that hall remain the primary record of how the man actually worked, because the teacher at the front of the room is seventy-six and the people running the cameras have understood that there will not be many more chances at this. He understands it at least as well as they do.
stops.quote: Nothing is permanent about our behavior patterns except our belief that they are so.
stops.quote_source: Widely attributed to Feldenkrais and often assigned to Awareness Through Movement; edition unconfirmed, not verified against a primary text.
suggested_refs: The Amherst training recordings, 1980-1981

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the fall and the end of teaching
stops.date_confidence: attested: he becomes seriously ill and stops public teaching after two of four planned summer sessions. The illness follows a fall in 1981 and involves a subdural hematoma and subsequent strokes. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: A fall, a subdural hematoma, and strokes after it. He stops teaching in public. The Amherst training continues without him and is finished by his own students, which is what the thirteen in Tel Aviv and the sixty-five in San Francisco were for. He spends three years unable to do for himself the thing he spent forty years teaching other people to do, and no account of those years records him complaining about the arrangement. Segal and the first thirteen are carrying the work now, in four countries, without him.
stops.quote: In short, health is measured by the shock a person can take without his usual way of life being compromised.
stops.quote_source: Widely attributed to Feldenkrais and commonly assigned to Awareness Through Movement; edition unconfirmed, not verified against a primary text.
suggested_refs: Medical and personal accounts of Feldenkrais's final illness, not located

stops.name: Tel Aviv, death at eighty
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1 July 1984, widely repeated; the underlying primary obituary was not read directly this pass.
stops.campa: He dies in Tel Aviv at eighty, in the city he helped raise out of dunes as a labourer of fifteen. Between the two facts sit a Paris doctorate, a black belt, a war spent hunting submarines under the Firth of Clyde, and a discipline now taught on four continents by people who never met him. A memorial plaque goes up on the house he lived in, and no source found gives its street or the date it was fixed to the wall. The guilds that certify his teachers outlive him by decades, and the evidence reviews that test his claims are still coming out forty years later, and they are mixed.
stops.quote: move closer to actually being creatures of free choice, to genuinely reflect individual creativity and emotion, freeing it of habitual tensions and wired patterns of behavior so that it may respond without inhibition
stops.quote_source: Interview with Moshé Feldenkrais, New Realities, vol. 1 (1977), read in Google Books snippet. The version in wide circulation alters three words and prefixes an opener he does not appear to have said.
suggested_refs: The memorial plaque on Feldenkrais's Tel Aviv house, street address not located

stops.name: Givatayim, the grave that is not certain
stops.date_confidence: [R] and contested. Nahalat Yitzhak is given only by an uncited Wikipedia category tag, and the cemetery's own article does not list him among notable burials; another assertion in circulation names Kiryat Shaul instead. Unresolved. The date is the customary interval, not a record. Coordinate corrected by 1.4 km.
stops.campa: He is buried, according to the better of two weak claims, at Nahalat Yitzhak in Givatayim, on the eastern edge of the city. The cemetery's own roll of notable dead does not name him. A second account puts him at Kiryat Shaul instead. For a man who spent his working life telling people to verify things in their own experience rather than take them on authority, the record of where he lies is a category tag on an encyclopedia page with nothing underneath it.
